nexusClaim.associationBasis: Authoring registers this relationship only as the bounded association the located thyroid literature supports: a 2021 JAMA Psychiatry systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 studies and 348,014 participants reports hypothyroidism associated with clinical depression at OR 1.30 (95 percent CI 1.08-1.57), stronger in overt hypothyroidism (OR 1.77, 95 percent CI 1.13-2.77) than in subclinical hypothyroidism (OR 1.13, 95 percent CI 1.01-1.28), with sensitivity analyses yielding MORE CONSERVATIVE estimates, an inconclusive autoimmunity coprimary (OR 1.24, 95 percent CI 0.89-1.74), and a post hoc signal in female individuals (OR 1.48, 95 percent CI 1.18-1.85) that is NULL in male individuals (OR 0.71, 95 percent CI 0.40-1.25) (PMID 34524390); a 2019 meta-analysis of seven studies and 103,375 subjects reports subclinical hypothyroidism associated with elevated depression risk (OR 1.78, 95 percent CI 1.11-2.86, P 0.02), most marked above age 50 (PMID 31214119); while a 2018 meta-analysis of subclinical hypothyroidism reports the composite endpoint NOT significant (SMD 0.23, 95 percent CI -0.03 to 0.48, P 0.08) and the depressive-diagnosis odds ratio not significant (OR 1.75, 95 percent CI 0.97-3.17, P 0.064), with a younger-than-60 subgroup signal (OR 3.8, 95 percent CI 1.02-14.18) and an older-adult null, and NO antidepressant effect of levothyroxine supplementation (SMD 0.26, 95 percent CI -0.09 to 0.62, P 0.143) (PMID 30375372). The registered claim is the narrowest these anchors jointly permit: that hypothyroidism is associated with clinical depression at a modest pooled odds ratio, with the located effect concentrated in overt hypothyroidism and female populations, and with the two subclinical meta-analyses in DIRECT CONFLICT on whether any association exists at all.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation of depression is established for any individual: every anchor is an epidemiologic meta-analysis of prevalence or odds, so none establishes that the thyroid dysfunction precedes the depression in an individual; the primary anchor's own authors conclude the effect size is CONSIDERABLY LOWER THAN PREVIOUSLY ASSUMED and possibly restricted to overt hypothyroidism and female individuals, its sensitivity analyses are more conservative than its headline, and its autoimmunity coprimary is inconclusive; the two subclinical meta-analyses CONFLICT (OR 1.78 positive versus composite SMD 0.23 and OR 1.75 both not significant) and disagree on which age group carries any signal (above 50 in one, below 60 in the other); the levothyroxine-treatment meta-analysis reports NO improvement of depression with thyroid-hormone supplementation in subclinical hypothyroidism, which is explicit counterweight against a simple hormone-deficiency causal reading; the female-only post hoc signal leaves a male null (OR 0.71 crossing 1). Individual claims require independently established hypothyroidism with dated thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) predating the depressive diagnosis, exclusion of euthyroid-sick phenomenon, of medication effects (lithium, amiodarone, immune checkpoint inhibitors), of postpartum and autoimmune thyroiditis trajectories, and of primary psychosocial etiologies before any attribution.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized neuroendocrine pathway: reduced thyroid hormone action is held to impair central monoaminergic function and neurotrophic signaling (the long-recognized hypothyroid-"pseudodysthymia" presentation), the route the overt-stronger-than-subclinical gradient is consistent with; but the levothyroxine-treatment null means the pathway cannot be treated as demonstrated by hormone replacement response, so whether thyroid dysfunction produced any individual's depression remains hypothesized until the endocrine and psychiatric chronology is read together.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Held at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at meta-analytic epidemiologic class with the anchor conflicts carried openly rather than resolved: the pooled OR of 1.30 is modest and its own authors stress it is lower than previously assumed; the subclinical literature is split, one meta-analysis positive (OR 1.78) and one composite-null (SMD 0.23, OR 1.75 not significant); the treatment evidence (levothyroxine no antidepressant effect, P 0.143) is a direct counterweight to causal reading and is registered as such; the female-only post hoc signal with male null bounds the claim to female populations. Target window note: the registry already carries this file's outgoing hypothyroidism to tinnitus edge and the batch-80 bipolar-disorder to hypothyroidism lithium edge arrives at this identity from a PHARMACOLOGICAL_IATROGENIC route, so a mood window FROM this identity is directionally distinct from the lithium-mediated mood windows and is not a duplicate of them; the batch-80 ptsd to hypothyroidism shared-lithium-route refusal is untouched by this edge.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: NO located anchor establishes onset order between hypothyroidism and depression; the two subclinical meta-analyses conflict in both magnitude and age direction; the primary anchor's sensitivity analyses are more conservative than its headline OR, its autoimmunity coprimary is inconclusive, and its strongest signal is a POST HOC female-only analysis with a male null; the levothyroxine-treatment meta-analysis reports no antidepressant effect; and no anchor reports incident depression in a thyroid-function-confirmed hypothyroid cohort free of baseline psychiatric disease.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Primary major depressive disorder with secondary neuroendocrine effects on thyroid indices
Lithium, amiodarone and immune-checkpoint-inhibitor thyroid injury as exogenous causes of the hypothyroidism
Euthyroid-sick phenomenon and transient thyroiditis misread as stable hypothyroidism
Psychosocial stressors, chronic medical illness burden and unemployment/disability as depression drivers in a population with chronic endocrine disease
Postpartum thyroiditis trajectories in the female-skewed populations the strongest signals come from

sourceReferences.citation: Bode H, Ivens B, Bschor T, Schwarzer G, Henssler J, Baethge C. Association of Hypothyroidism and Clinical Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2021 Dec 1;78(12):1375-1383. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2021.2506. PMID 34524390.
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis, 25 studies, 348,014 participants, registered as the PRIMARY anchor: hypothyroidism with clinical depression OR 1.30 (95 percent CI 1.08-1.57); overt OR 1.77 (1.13-2.77) versus subclinical OR 1.13 (1.01-1.28); autoimmunity coprimary inconclusive OR 1.24 (0.89-1.74); sensitivity analyses more conservative; post hoc female OR 1.48 (1.18-1.85) with male NULL OR 0.71 (0.40-1.25). Authors conclude the effect is considerably lower than previously assumed and possibly restricted to overt hypothyroidism and female individuals. DISCLOSURE CARRIED: Dr Schwarzer reports personal fees from Roche Pharma outside the submitted work. Mapping approval is not citation verification; this source enters verified:false pending qualified-human citation review.
